description: Six students from NIT Bhopal building the CLPS Lunar Mission Browser. Team: 3 software developers, 1 core-logic developer, 1 IoT/hardware developer (ESP32), 1 design/docs/pitch member. We're building a web tool to compare lunar south pole landing sites and dates, showing Sun/Earth positions, power potential and Earth-comms windows, plus a small physical device that mirrors the data
summary:
**CLPS LUNA BROWSER**
*Lunar Landing-Site Analysis & Hardware Demonstration*

CLPS Luna Browser is an integrated software and hardware platform designed to explore and compare potential lunar south-pole landing sites through scientific data, AI-assisted analysis, and physical visualization.

**SOFTWARE**
Built using React, TypeScript, Three.js, Python, FastAPI, and PostgreSQL, the platform features nine selected lunar locations. Peak near Cabeus B and Haworth have detailed research profiles. Site Comparison evaluates available parameters such as terrain, scientific value, potential water ice, and sunlight. AI Assist uses a locally hosted Ollama model to interpret natural-language queries and generate structured criteria. Scientific processing incorporates SPICE, DE440, and LOLA datasets where available.

**HARDWARE — CODEX**
CODEX is a physical demonstrator featuring an ESP32 Base Station and an ESP32-S3 Moon Module. It integrates an Arduino Uno, CNC Shield V3, NEMA 17 and BYJ stepper motors, and 26 WS2812B LEDs representing 13 lunar regions. UART enables communication between the base station and motor controller, while the ESP32-S3 manages LED visualization.

**OUTCOME**
The project combines lunar research, AI, 3D visualization, embedded communication, and physical control into one integrated engineering prototype, connecting digital analysis with real-world demonstration.
details:
CLPS Luna Browser is an integrated software and hardware prototype for exploring and comparing potential lunar south-pole landing sites. It combines scientific data, AI-assisted search, 3D visualization, and a physical demonstrator.

The software includes nine locations, with detailed profiles for Peak near Cabeus B and Haworth. Site Comparison evaluates available factors such as terrain, scientific value, potential water ice, sunlight, and accessibility. AI Assist uses a local Ollama model to interpret natural-language requests and create structured criteria; the backend retrieves data and performs evaluations. Scientific processing uses SPICE, DE440, and LOLA data where available.

The hardware demonstrator, CODEX, represents a Base Station and Moon Module. An ESP32 serves as the Base Station, while an ESP32-S3 controls the Moon Module's LEDs. It also includes an Arduino Uno, CNC Shield V3, NEMA 17 and BYJ motors, and 26 WS2812B LEDs representing 13 lunar regions. UART connects the ESP32 and Arduino.

Tools include React, TypeScript, Three.js, Python, FastAPI, PostgreSQL, Ollama, ESP32, and Arduino.

Our creative approach connects digital lunar research with a physical model. We considered terrain safety, scientific value, potential water ice, sunlight, accessibility, data availability, and reliability. The project aims to make lunar research accessible, support preliminary site comparison, and demonstrate how AI, scientific computing, visualization, and embedded systems can work together for future exploration.
